# Appendix B Human-supervised AI-assisted research

## B1 Purpose of the methodological account

AI assistance was used to support the development and examination of Model
Agrologistic, while the researchers retained responsibility for the scientific
problem, the mathematical formulation and the interpretation of results.
This appendix explains how that division of work operated. Its purpose is to
make the research process understandable and inspectable, rather than to
attribute scientific authority to an assistant or to measure gains in productivity.

The mathematical foundation remains attributed to Rosa (2026). Consultations
with Gurobot occurred partly in parallel with that research; they do not
establish an independent origin for the model. The coauthors' meeting guidance
of 21 October 2026 requested an account of the tools, supervision and limitations
of AI assistance. The available meeting excerpt and historical source assessment
are identified in the [supporting research record](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic/blob/c092fa7be2fea69f6e0eb8ab707e38aa68e1b85b/docs/s6a_20261021/meeting_and_source_review.md).

We distinguish three kinds of material. Discussions document the questions and
alternatives considered. Versioned code and tests show what was implemented
and examined. Original experiment records establish what was actually executed
and returned. These sources answer different questions: a plausible proposal
does not establish a correct implementation, and a correct implementation does
not establish that a particular large experiment succeeded.

## B2 Assistance and human responsibility

Gurobot supported early formulation and implementation discussions. Gemini and
GPT systems were subsequently used to examine mathematical interpretations,
computational alternatives and possible inconsistencies. ChatGPT Classic
supported planning and editorial coordination. Codex assisted with Python
implementation, tests, diagnostics, execution scripts and documentation.
Historical records identify particular model versions where available; they
do not establish a complete chronology of every interaction.

The researchers evaluated the relevance of these proposals before adoption.
For mathematical work, this included examining indexing, units, first-stage
decisions, scenario probabilities and objective components. For computational
work, analytical examples and regression tests were followed by checks of the
returned large-instance evidence. The researcher executed NPAD commands and
transferred the resulting files; assistants did not acquire authority to launch
additional experiments from the success or failure of an earlier one.

Python, Gurobi, SCIP, Pyomo and HiGHS perform implementation or optimization
functions and are distinct from generative AI assistants. GitHub records
changes, while Slurm schedules computational work on NPAD. Keeping these roles
separate matters: a scheduler's successful exit reports completion of a
process, whereas acceptance of a solution requires examining its mathematical
and numerical evidence. Human authors retain responsibility for both decisions.

## B3 Historical formulation and exploratory work

The researcher supplied an expanded retrospective account produced by Gurobot.
It describes five phases of early assistance, summarized in Table B.1. The
account is useful for reconstructing the subjects discussed, but it is not an
original execution log or a complete transcript. Its numerical statements are
therefore reported as historical claims, without being added to the article's
accepted experimental cohort.

| Phase | Reported assistance and its relation to the present study |
| --- | --- |
| Initial formulation | Discussion of DET/STO structure and a synthetic example with two origins, three hubs, two destinations, two products, three periods and three scenarios. The account reports 513 variables and 261 constraints; these counts have not been independently reproduced here. |
| Model development | Exploration of investment activation, capacity expansion, eligibility and operational feasibility. The current model follows its explicitly defined rules; exploratory suggestions do not introduce an additional budget constraint. |
| GAMS exploration | Interpretation of an extended GAMS model, export outlets and a revenue-oriented objective, with reported counts of 1,710 variables and 936 constraints. These statements do not change the present cost-minimization objective. |
| Python/Pyomo translation | Discussion of the Rosa-related specification, Excel ingestion and implementation checks. Earlier distance approximations and information-value calculations are historical activities, rather than the current OSRM/scalar method. |
| Benders exploration | Proposals concerning decomposition, bounds, indices and warm starts. Their retrospective description is not a reproduced decomposition experiment or a result of the evaluated extensive-form implementation. |

: Table B.1. Topics described in the researcher-supplied Gurobot retrospective.

This distinction preserves the usefulness of the historical account without
overstating its evidentiary strength. In particular, a retrospective statement
that code ran in a sandbox cannot replace a retained solver log, input identity
and numerical validation report. Unavailable dates, model versions and
conversation contents have not been reconstructed.

## B4 Verification through the research workflow

The workflow in Figure B.1 begins with a scientific question and a provisional
proposal. Human evaluation determines whether the proposal fits the problem.
An adopted proposal is implemented under version control and examined using
small examples with known answers, software tests and checks of the
mathematical formulation. Large experiments then use explicitly specified
inputs, resource limits and solver settings.

![Figure B.1. Human-supervised research workflow. Proposals are reviewed before implementation; tests and original experiment evidence support subsequent interpretation. Return arrows represent revision when a discrepancy is found.](../figures/human_ai_workflow.png)

The numerical checks address more than the reported objective. They examine
local material balances, investment eligibility, scenario-specific constraints,
the units of each slack and the reconstruction of costs from exported
decisions. Investment must be charged once, even when operating variables are
replicated across scenarios. An aggregate balance cannot compensate for a
local violation. Likewise, a small gap for the penalized objective does not
establish accurate financial costs or adequate service when artificial penalties
dominate that objective.

After an experiment, the original outputs are retained together with the
source version, input and population identities, settings, resource
observations and terminal accounting. Replaying these records can verify
their consistency and integrity. It does not constitute a new optimization or
a fresh residual evaluation against private inputs. This separation allows
later editorial corrections without changing the evidence generated by an
earlier execution.

## B5 Decisions that illustrate the supervision process

The restoration of the scalar objective illustrates why human mathematical
review remained necessary. An earlier hierarchical implementation could run
successfully without representing the economic comparison approved for this
study. The researchers required a single scalar objective and excluded
information-value calculations from the active campaign. Analytical tests then
examined the placement of investment costs, the three penalties and the
deterministic specialization of the stochastic implementation. The correction
concerned the scientific meaning of the calculation, rather than merely
whether the software executed.

The treatment of penalties provides a second example. Their large contribution
to the objective prompted a proposal for calibration. The researcher retained
the approved effective rates of 90000/45000/45000 for the bounded computational
study. Subsequent interpretation therefore separates financial expenditure,
artificial penalties and physical shortages or capacity exceedances. The
workflow did not turn a modeling limitation into an unperformed sensitivity
analysis or silently change coefficients to obtain more attractive results.

Operational supervision also led to revisions. An initially stronger execution-
isolation design required host capabilities unavailable in the academic
environment. Diagnostic failures were retained, and the researcher adopted a
proportionate procedure based on bounded resources, identified processes and
inspectable records. This change improved the relevance of the execution
protocol without certifying unavailable production-isolation properties.
Similarly, population preparation was checked against original facility
identifiers and ranking records after an unsuitable path or interpretation
blocked an earlier attempt.

These examples describe observable decisions and their consequences.
Detailed commit, test and experiment identities remain in the
[versioned development record](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic/pulls?q=is%3Apr+state%3Aclosed).
They support reconstruction of the decisions without turning the supplement
into a chronological catalogue of software administration.

## B6 Limits and implications

The available conversations are incomplete, and retrospective accounts can
contain errors. Different assistants may rely on the same source or repeat
one another's mistake; agreement among them is not independent scientific
review. Commit records and passing tests do not identify the authorship of
every line of code. The study has no counterfactual design for estimating time
saved, improvements in productivity or reductions in error attributable to AI.

The methodological value of the workflow is consequently bounded. It connects
proposals to human decisions, implementations and evidence that another
researcher can inspect. It does not reveal hidden language-model reasoning or
guarantee correctness. Restricted inputs may still limit independent
reproduction, and final scientific interpretation and publication require
coauthor review. Formal authorship and CRediT assignments remain decisions of
the human authors.
